claim: Previous reports have described worsening inequalities of National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding.
source: Previous reports have described worsening inequalities of National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding.
evidence: This claim references prior literature on NIH funding inequalities, indicating it is supported by citations to other work.

claim: Worsening inequalities in NIH funding began at the time of the NIH budget doubling (1998–2003).
source: We analyzed Research Project Grant data through the end of Fiscal Year 2020, confirming worsening inequalities beginning at the time of the NIH budget doubling (1998–2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis of RPG data showing temporal patterns in inequality measures.

claim: Trends in funding inequalities have reversed in recent years for both investigators and institutions, but only to a modest degree.
source: We analyzed Research Project Grant data through the end of Fiscal Year 2020, confirming worsening inequalities beginning at the time of the NIH budget doubling (1998–2003), while finding that trends in recent years have reversed for both investigators and institutions, but only to a modest degree.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of RPG data through FY2020.

claim: Career-stage trends have stabilized, with equivalent proportions of early-, mid-, and late-career investigators funded from 2017 to 2020.
source: We also find that career-stage trends have stabilized, with equivalent proportions of early-, mid-, and late-career investigators funded from 2017 to 2020.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of career stage distribution data.

claim: The fraction of women among funded PIs continues to increase, but they are still not at parity.
source: The fraction of women among funded PIs continues to increase, but they are still not at parity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis of gender distribution data over time.

claim: Inequalities for investigators have consistently been greater within groups than between groups.
source: Analyses of funding inequalities show that inequalities for investigators, and to a lesser degree for institutions, have consistently been greater within groups (i.e. within groups by career stage, gender, race, and degree) than between groups.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' Theil index decomposition analysis.

claim: Inequalities for institutions have consistently been greater within groups than between groups, to a lesser degree than for investigators.
source: Analyses of funding inequalities show that inequalities for investigators, and to a lesser degree for institutions, have consistently been greater within groups (i.e. within groups by career stage, gender, race, and degree) than between groups.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' Theil index decomposition analysis for institutions.

claim: There has been increasing interest in how NIH funding support is distributed over the past few years.
source: Over the past few years, there has been increasing interest (Peifer, 2017) in how the National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding support is distributed
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peifer, 2017.

claim: There is concern that there may be excess concentration of NIH support given to men and to the most well-funded late-career investigators.
source: Over the past few years, there has been increasing interest (Peifer, 2017) in how the National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding support is distributed, with concern voiced by some that there may be excess concentration of support given to men and to the most well-funded late-career investigators.
evidence: This claim is based on concerns voiced in the literature, as indicated by the citation.

claim: In biomedical science, power stems from who has access to awards.
source: In a report (National Institutes of Health, 2019) issued by an NIH Working Group to the Advisory Committee to the Director (ACD), it was noted that "In biomedical science, power stems from who has access to awards.
evidence: This claim is quoted from an NIH Working Group report.

claim: The concentration of funding in a relatively small number of investigators (who are overwhelmingly white, cisgender, straight men) incentivizes universities to protect researchers bringing in high levels of grant funding.
source: The Working Group heard repeatedly that the concentration of funding in a relatively small number of investigators (who are overwhelmingly white, cisgender, straight men) incentivizes universities to protect researchers bringing in high levels of grant funding
evidence: This claim is from an NIH Working Group report cited in the text.

claim: There has been increasing inequality of NIH funding support over 30 years (1985–2015) for all 'R' grants.

claim: Women identified as Principal Investigators receive lower levels of support for grants.

claim: There is disproportionate aging of the research workforce.

claim: Mid-career investigators experience particular stresses.

claim: There is no correlation between research stage and scientific impact.

claim: In 2017, the NIH considered imposing a cap on individual-investigator research support through use of a 'Grant Support Index or GSI'.

claim: The GSI classified grants according to mechanism (e.g. R01, P01, U54) rather than according to dollars.

claim: The GSI set a value of 7 for R01 grants, with lower values for 'smaller' mechanisms like R03 or R21 and greater values for mechanisms like P01 or U54.

claim: The proposed GSI cap was highly controversial.
